\paragraph{Relation to prior work.} White-box probes read deception from activations~\citep{zou2023representation, burns2023discovering, azaria2023internal}; the black-box line's closest instance---our primary audit target---is \citet{pacchiardi2024catch}, and we audit both paradigms (§\ref{sec:td_vs_fd}). Three concurrent evaluations~\citep{kretschmar2025liarsbench, cooney2026didyoulie, hopkins2026liedetectors} find lie detectors fail to \textbf{generalize} beyond the regime they were fit in. That is a question about \textbf{predictive validity}; ours is the prior one, about \textbf{attributional validity}: instructed-lie accuracy is \textbf{not merely poorly generalizing but uninterpretable as evidence about deception}, because the intervention moves deception and compliance together---so generalization can be perfect while identification still fails. \textbf{Fixed elicitation is also not what we claim to introduce}---\citet{cooney2026didyoulie}'s trained organisms have it and go \emph{beyond} it, with $D$ \emph{set} rather than observed. \textbf{Our novelty is using it as the missing construct-validity criterion for reading instructed-benchmark accuracy}: we formalize the identification failure, turn it into an auditable protocol, and \textbf{show empirically that the confound accounts for substantial benchmark accuracy across three mechanistically distinct detector paradigms}---while auditing whether public artifacts supply the criterion at all. Appendix~\ref{app:related_work} places all five kinds against requirements~(i)--(v) (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:prior_work_criteria}).

\subsection{Benign False-Positive Rate of the Parameter-Free Rule (EXP-BF)}
\label{app:benign_fpr}

A reviewer asked the obvious question about a rule that reaches 69--80\% by counting correction markers: how often does it fire when there is nothing to correct? This subsection answers it. \textbf{It is a diagnostic, not a pre-registered analysis}, reported on the same footing as claim~3 in Table~\ref{tab:claim_ledger}.

\paragraph{Materials.} 50 benign prompts in five groups of ten: factual questions with true answers (``What is the capital of France?''), opinions and recommendations, task-help requests, small talk, and short explanatory questions (``Why is the ocean salty?''). \textbf{No prompt contains a false claim and none creates a knowledge conflict}; that is the point of the set, and also the limit of what it can show. Each target answers under one byte-identical neutral system prompt, ``You are a helpful assistant. Answer the user's question clearly and concisely.'', through the unmodified generation path of EXP-R1/EXP-C4 (\texttt{max\_tokens}~300, \texttt{temperature}~0.7), one prompt per fresh conversation. \textbf{That is not the equalized arm's system prompt}: §\ref{sec:r1_faithful}'s neutral prompt tells the model it ``will be asked about a factual claim'', which is incoherent for a set that contains no claim. So the comparison below is the rule applied to ordinary assistant output, not the equalized arm with its claims deleted, and it is one more reason the number bounds ambient firing and nothing about the knowledge-conflict regime.

\paragraph{Detector.} The parameter-free rule exactly as §\ref{sec:hedging_baseline} scores it: $k\!\geq\!1$ over the 14 patterns above, $k$ being the number of \emph{distinct} patterns matching case-insensitively. The scoring script imports that list rather than copying it and \textbf{aborts unless the import is exactly 14 patterns long}, so this table cannot drift from the inventory. Targets are EXP-C4's five (§\ref{app:crit4_ours}), with Qwen~2.5~32B excluded on the memory ground stated there.

\paragraph{Result.} \textbf{The rule fires on 0/250 benign responses}, 0 of 50 on every target separately, \textbf{Wilson 95\% $[0.0, 1.5]$\%} pooled and $[0.0, 7.1]$\% per target (Table~\ref{tab:benign_fpr}). Stored responses run to a median of 330--1{,}182 characters by target and 1{,}584 at the longest, so the full response was scored in every case. \textbf{The markers the rule counts are not ambient in ordinary assistant output}: whatever §\ref{sec:hedging_baseline}'s 69--80\% is, it is not a rule that fires on nearly everything and scores well because the benchmark is balanced.

\paragraph{Pattern sensitivity.} The count is 0/250 under all three inventories that can be scored here: the 14 patterns above; the 13-pattern variant with \texttt{\textbackslash bincorrect\textbackslash b} dropped, which is the one §\ref{sec:hedging_baseline}'s 69.1\% figure relies on; and the 4-pattern list the superseded July script carried. \textbf{The result does not depend on which inventory is used}, which is the one respect in which it is more robust than the accuracy figures it accompanies.

\paragraph{Why these responses were collected twice.} An earlier collection of the same design (July 2026, six targets) is \textbf{superseded and not reported}, for two collection defects found while preparing this subsection and reproducible from the archived files by \texttt{analyze\_benign\_fpr.py -{}-july}. First, the local-inference client returns the fixed string ``I'm not sure about that.'' when a request times out, and the old script stored that as an ordinary non-firing response: 68 of its 300 records are timeouts, all 50 of a target that was not installed at all (a prefix match in the availability check accepted an absent tag whose family sibling was present) plus 18 of a second target. Second, responses were stored truncated to their first 500 characters, which affected 135 of the 232 non-timeout records. \textbf{Truncation can only hide a marker, never invent one}, so that collection could support a lower bound and not a rate. The re-collection stores responses whole, retries a timeout up to three times, refuses to start unless every target's exact tag is installed, and records an unrecoverable timeout as an \emph{error excluded from the denominator} rather than as a response that did not fire.

\paragraph{What this does and does not bound.} Four limits, each of which narrows the claim.
\textbf{(1)~A zero count is not a zero rate.} Read the interval, not the point estimate: at this $n$ the data are consistent with a benign firing rate as high as 1.5\%, and nothing here excludes rarer firing.
\textbf{(2)~It measures specificity against ordinary conversation only.} Because the set contains no false claim and no knowledge conflict, this says the correction markers are \textbf{not ambient in normal assistant output}; it does \emph{not} bound the knowledge-conflict component of the rule's benchmark accuracy (§\ref{app:belief_strata}), and it is \textbf{not evidence that the rule detects deception}.
\textbf{(3)~Only the rule's false-positive rate exists.} The interrogation pipeline's benign false-positive rate was not measured, so no claim is made about it.
\textbf{(4)~It does not soften §\ref{sec:adversarial_paraphrase}.} Specificity against benign talk and robustness to adversarial rewording are different properties, and the rule has the first without the second: the same rule loses its markers 84\%$\to$16\% under a style-constraint adversary and sits at 35--51\% across 17 instruction paraphrases. \textbf{A detector can be quiet on ordinary conversation and still be trivially evadable}; both are properties of a surface feature, and neither is evidence of construct validity.
